query: A Question in the Margin The essay is back on the stair, bleeding red. Most of it is about your argument. At the bottom, smaller: "Why do you want to be good at this?" It's the first question the ink has asked. Answer it honestly in the margin You write three lines you'd never say aloud, and leave the essay on the stair. It's gone by noon. You spend the afternoon wishing you'd written two. Wait on the stair to see who takes it You hide on the landing above. A first-year in robes two sizes too big gathers up the pages, reads the first line right there on the step, and makes a small, furious noise. You fall asleep on the stair. When you wake the essay is gone, and there's a note on your chest in red: "Paragraph six. Also, you snore."

Still Waiting
There's a note in red ink tucked into the crack in the lecture tower stair, in the small round hand you know. It says only: "Still waiting for the next draft. Paragraph four is still the best thing you've written. Don't make it the last."
